enrichment.short_title: Pedestrian's contributory negligence reduced from 60% to 40% where driver bore greater causative potency
key_facts: A 17-year-old pedestrian was very seriously injured when struck by a car on Marine Parade, Great Yarmouth, at night in June 1989.
She had walked along the carriageway for some time, refused warnings to get off the road, and was in the offside lane when struck.
The driver was in the offside lane at about 30–35 mph, had consumed enough alcohol to impair his driving, and failed to see or avoid her despite good visibility.
Moses J found the driver liable but apportioned 60% contributory negligence to the claimant; the only challenged finding was that she was 'drunk', which the Court of Appeal held was unsupported.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claimant's appeal to the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) against a High Court apportionment of contributory negligence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; contributory negligence substituted at 40%; costs on an indemnity basis.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 1(1) of the 1945 Act the court must do what is just and equitable by comparing both parties' causative potency and blameworthiness; it is rare for a pedestrian to be found more responsible than a driver unless they suddenly move into the path of a vehicle, and a qualitative difference exists between findings of 60% and 40% contribution.
legal_issues: Whether the trial judge was plainly wrong to hold the claimant more responsible than the defendant
How causative potency and blameworthiness should be balanced under the 1945 Act
Whether the finding that the claimant was drunk was supported by evidence

enrichment.short_title: Appeal conditioned on payment of interim costs where impecunious company delayed enforcement
key_facts: Contract Facilities Ltd, restored to the register with retrospective effect, lost at trial a claim for specific performance or damages relating to a share purchase contract and was ordered to pay costs.
The company had no assets; Mr Shuck funded the litigation and used procedural tactics to postpone detailed assessment and enforcement before the appeal was heard.
Security for costs on the appeal was provided ten minutes late; an interim costs certificate for £37,000 and further costs orders remained unpaid.
The respondents applied for dismissal of the appeal or for payment of outstanding costs as a condition of pursuing the appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Respondents' application to the Court of Appeal during the currency of Contract Facilities Ltd's appeal against a county court order.
enrichment.outcome: Unless Contract paid £37,000 into court and £2,000 and £4,792 to the respondents by 18 July 2003, the appeal would be struck out; respondents' costs of the application also ordered.
enrichment.ratio: The Court of Appeal has case management powers under CPR 2.1 and 3.1 to impose conditions on a pending appeal where a funded appellant seeks to prosecute an appeal while disobeying costs orders and there is no real risk of stifling; this is distinct from an application to vary permission to appeal at first instance under CPR 52.9.
legal_issues: Whether the Court of Appeal had jurisdiction to impose payment conditions on a pending appeal
Whether CPR 52.9(3) prevented imposing conditions after permission was granted in the respondents' presence
Whether requiring payment of past costs as a condition of appeal prejudged a section 51 application against the funder

enrichment.short_title: Inspector's grant of guest-house reconversion upheld; prematurity refusal and costs award lawful
key_facts: Mrs Delabatouche applied to convert upper floors of Sherebourne, Tenby, from guest-house use into two flats without local-needs occupancy restrictions.
Pembrokeshire Coast National Park Authority refused permission on prematurity grounds to protect emerging draft policy 47 restricting unrestricted housing in the national park.
The inspector allowed the appeal, giving little weight to the emerging policy and awarding costs against the authority for unreasonable conduct.
The authority challenged both the planning decision and the costs award under section 288.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under section 288 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990, with a linked judicial review of the inspector's costs order.
enrichment.outcome: Section 288 challenge dismissed; challenge to the costs order dismissed; claimant ordered to pay defendants' agreed costs of £8,149.50.
enrichment.ratio: Prematurity is not an automatic trump card where an emerging policy is controversial and not deposited with strong evidential support; a decision-maker may lawfully attach little weight to an emerging local-needs housing policy and refuse prematurity where the proposal is a small internal reconversion with limited cumulative impact, and may award costs where the authority acted unreasonably in refusing permission.
legal_issues: Whether the inspector erred in attaching little weight to emerging draft policy 47
Whether prematurity was established for a two-unit reconversion in Tenby
Whether cumulative precedent effects were adequately addressed
Whether the inspector lawfully awarded costs for unreasonable conduct

enrichment.short_title: Employment tribunal chairman's link to counsel instructed by employer did not require recusal
key_facts: Mr Jones, a senior claims handler at DAS Legal Expenses Insurance Co Ltd, brought sex discrimination and victimisation claims before an employment tribunal.
At the outset the chairman disclosed that her barrister husband's chambers undertook work for DAS and that he had occasionally been instructed by the respondent; Mr Jones did not object.
After dismissal of his claims he investigated and found Mr Harper had been directly instructed on several occasions and paid fees of about £3,000 in the year before the hearing.
The Employment Appeal Tribunal rejected bias and perversity grounds; Mr Jones appealed to the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on alleged bias and lack of impartiality.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed with costs summarily assessed at £1,000.
enrichment.ratio: A tribunal chairman whose spouse occasionally received modest panel work from the respondent does not have the requisite direct financial interest for automatic disqualification; applying Porter v Magill, a fair-minded informed observer would not conclude there was a real possibility of bias, and where adequate disclosure was made the litigant in person waived objection by continuing after adjournment with full knowledge of the essential facts.
legal_issues: Whether presumed bias arose from the chairman's spouse's occasional instructions by DAS
Whether apparent bias was established under Porter v Magill
Whether Mr Jones validly waived the disclosed conflict
What procedural steps tribunals should take when a conflict emerges at the start of a hearing

enrichment.short_title: Auditors' duty to bond insurer arguable where travel agent's accounts were known to support ABTA/IATA applications
key_facts: IAIC provided ABTA and IATA bonds and loans to Swift Travel, relying on audited accounts prepared by Michael Cook & Co.
Swift Travel later ceased trading; IAIC suffered losses and investigation costs and alleged the auditors negligently prepared materially misleading financial statements.
The auditors applied to strike out or obtain summary judgment on the ground that no duty of care was owed to IAIC.
Mr Justice Lloyd refused the application, holding the pleaded case arguable on proximity and scope of duty.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal against refusal of strike-out/summary judgment application.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; claim allowed to proceed to trial.
enrichment.ratio: In auditor liability, where the pleaded facts allege the auditors knew audited statements would be supplied to institutions such as the claimant to obtain bond facilities and would be relied on, the case is at the margin of existing authority and should not be struck out under CPR 3.4(2)(a); the law in this field remains incrementally developing and is fact-sensitive.

Whether proximity and assumption of responsibility were sufficiently pleaded
Whether the claim was plainly covered by Al Saudi Banque and Caparo
Whether CPR 24.2 added anything where all facts were taken from the particulars of claim

enrichment.short_title: Drug importation trial fair despite refusal of visas for Nigerian defence witnesses
key_facts: The appellant was stopped at Gatwick with cocaine and heroin concealed in a false bottom of a wheelie bag she said had been given to her in Nigeria by Mama Chardy.
Two Nigerian witnesses supported her account in statements taken by her solicitor, but visa applications to attend trial were refused.
The trial judge refused a stay; the witnesses' statements were read under section 23 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 with an appropriate jury direction.
She was convicted by a 10:2 majority and sentenced to eleven and a half years' imprisonment on each count concurrent.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) against conviction following refusal of a stay for alleged unfairness.
enrichment.ratio: Refusal of entry visas for defence witnesses does not automatically breach Article 6 where their statements are admitted under section 23 and the jury receives a proper direction; a trial judge is not required to review immigration decisions, and fairness depends on whether the trial process as a whole remained fair on the central issue of knowledge.
legal_issues: Whether Customs and Excise failed to assist sufficiently in obtaining visas
Whether the state was indivisible so visa refusal rendered the trial unfair
Whether reading statements under section 23 cured the restriction on calling witnesses
Whether the judge should have stayed proceedings as an abuse of process

enrichment.short_title: Dyslexia negligence claim held time-barred where knowledge accrued before majority
key_facts: Nicholas Rowe, born in 1974, was educated in Hull and Essex and diagnosed with dyslexia in March 1991.
He claimed local education authorities negligently failed to identify and ameliorate his dyslexia, causing personal injury and loss.
Writ issued in September 1998, more than three years after his eighteenth birthday in October 1992.
The trial judge held the claim not time-barred and said he would exercise section 33 discretion; the authorities appealed on limitation as a preliminary issue.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Defendants' appeal to the Court of Appeal from a High Court preliminary issue decision on limitation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; action held statute-barred; section 33 discretion refused; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Knowledge under section 14(1)(a) is of the fact of a significant injury, not of legal entitlement to sue; where a claimant knew before majority that he was dyslexic, remedial steps existed and had not been taken, time began at eighteen, and section 33 should not be exercised where the passage of time has substantially impaired the defendants' ability to defend stale school-negligence claims.
legal_issues: When the claimant acquired knowledge of a significant injury under section 14(1)(a)
Whether Phelps v Hillingdon changed the date of knowledge
Whether section 14 should be read compatibly with Article 6
Whether the judge misdirected himself in exercising section 33 discretion

enrichment.short_title: Loft bedroom grant refused where extra room would alleviate but not make home safe for autistic child

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996

key_facts: Mr and Mrs B sought a mandatory disabled facilities grant to convert their loft into an extra bedroom for their son DB, who has dyspraxia and Asperger's syndrome.
DB shared a bedroom with his brother SB and displayed aggressive behaviour at home, though school reports were more positive.
Occupational therapists concluded the main issue was overcrowding and behavioural management rather than a mandatory safety adaptation.
Calderdale refused the grant on the basis that the works were not within section 23(1)(b) and were not necessary and appropriate under section 24(3).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Calderdale Metropolitan Borough Council's refusal of a mandatory disabled facilities grant.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; permission to appeal granted.
enrichment.ratio: Section 23(1)(b) requires works whose purpose is to make the dwelling safe for the disabled occupant and others residing with him, not merely safer; where behavioural problems persist throughout the home, providing an extra bedroom may be beneficial but does not necessarily make the premises safe, and the authority lawfully distinguished mandatory safety grants from sleeping accommodation under paragraph (d).
legal_issues: Whether loft conversion fell within section 23(1)(b) mandatory purposes
Whether 'safe' means wholly safe or materially safer
Whether section 24(3) necessity and appropriateness were lawfully assessed
Whether irrelevant considerations rendered the decision unlawful

enrichment.short_title: Albanian blood-feud certification quashed where Secretary of State failed to weigh claim properly
key_facts: The Albanian claimant sought asylum/human rights protection based on a long-running family blood feud with the Dodaj family, including recent threats in Tirana.
Albania was listed under section 94(4); the Secretary of State certified the claim under section 94(3) as not clearly unfounded.
The claimant had reported threats to police and fled internally before leaving for the UK; objective country evidence showed continuing blood-feud killings and limited state protection.
The claimant had been removed to Albania before permission was granted, but the challenge proceeded through his father.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's section 94(3) certification.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; certification quashed; costs awarded to claimant; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: Certification under section 94(3) requires anxious scrutiny of the individual claim against objective country material; where blood-feud cases admit more than one legitimate view on sufficiency of protection, and the decision-maker gives insufficient weight to the depth of the feud and contemporaneous tribunal decisions such as Brozi and Koci, certification as clearly unfounded is unlawful.
legal_issues: The ZL & VL approach to section 94(3) certification
Whether sufficiency of protection in Albania was clearly established
Whether failure to use reconciliation services defeated the claim
Whether the Secretary of State adequately weighed the claimant's particular feud history

enrichment.short_title: Earl denied life interest in Shirburn Castle but entitled to two years' notice as licensee
key_facts: Shirburn Castle and estate are owned by Shirburn Estate Company Ltd, controlled by branches of the Parker/Macclesfield family.
In 1993 the Ninth Earl moved from Portobello Farm into the castle while negotiating, through Cluttons, for a tenancy at arm's length.
Family negotiations to grant him a life occupancy failed; the company served short notices to quit in 2002.
The Earl claimed proprietary estoppel/life occupancy; Fentville occupied the Old Stores and claimed similar rights.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary issues ordered by Master Price on the legal and equitable rights of the Earl and Fentville in the castle and Old Stores.
enrichment.outcome: Proprietary estoppel claim rejected; Earl and Fentville held to occupy as licensees requiring not less than two years' dated notice to vacate; short notices invalid.
enrichment.ratio: A vague expectation of life occupancy of part of a complex historic castle, coupled with a reserved right to reject arbitrator-determined lease terms, is too uncertain for proprietary estoppel; where occupation was granted to facilitate arm's-length lease negotiations, the occupier was a licensee revocable only on not less than two years' notice once negotiations broke down.
legal_issues: Whether the Earl established proprietary estoppel to a life interest in Shirburn Castle
Whether occupation was a tenancy or licence
What notice was required to terminate the licence
Whether section 320 of the Companies Act 1985 invalidated any arrangement
